passage:
Dear Ritu Didi,
Thank you for the photo of Nana at your wedding. I've stuck it inside my maths notebook.
It's been three months. Some days I'm fine, and then a song on the bus hits me like a wave. I get angry too: at the hospital, at Nana for not telling us he felt ill, at myself for skipping his birthday call to finish a game.
Yesterday Isha showed me a silly video in the library and I laughed out loud. Then I felt terrible, as if laughing meant I'd forgotten him.
Mum says laughing is allowed. We talk about Nana every Sunday over his favourite jalebi.
You asked me to tell you if the sad feeling spreads to everything. Right now it's mostly about Nana. I still like drawing and my friends. If that changes, I'll tell Mum and the school counsellor. Promise.
Love,
Nikita

qa.q: Where did Nikita stick the photo of Nana?
Why did Nikita feel terrible after laughing in the library?
qa.a: Nikita felt ashamed, as if laughing meant Nana had been forgotten.

qa.q: What choice has Nikita made in case the sadness spreads, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Nikita has promised to tell Mum and the school counsellor if the sadness spreads to everything, so help would come early.

qa.q: How might Ritu Didi feel reading that the sadness is still mostly about Nana?
qa.a: She may feel relieved that Nikita still enjoys drawing and friends, while staying ready to help if that changes.

grounding: It shows a teenager whose grief for a grandparent brings sadness, anger, guilt and ashamed laughter, still tied to the loss and eased by family support.

passage: People think the year after someone dies is just sad. For me it was messy. I'm Vandana, and Jagdish Sir coached our kabaddi team from the time I was eleven. When he died in the bus accident, I was angry first, at the driver, at the rain, at myself for sulking through our last practice instead of saying thanks. Then in our first match without him, I made a raid, the whole team screamed, and I laughed. On the ride home I felt sick with shame, like I'd betrayed him. For a while it was only about him, and I could carry that. But around March I stopped caring about anything, even drawing, and I kept thinking I was useless. My mum noticed I'd stopped eating with the family and booked a counsellor that same week. That helped a lot. Now when I laugh on the mat, I think he'd have laughed too.

qa.q: Which sport did Jagdish Sir coach?
Why did Vandana feel sick with shame on the ride home?
qa.a: Vandana had laughed after a raid in the first match without Jagdish Sir and felt that the laughter betrayed him.

qa.q: What was the turning point around March, and why did it matter?
qa.a: When Vandana stopped caring about anything and felt useless, Mum noticed and booked a counsellor that same week, getting help before things got worse.

qa.q: How might Vandana's mum have seen the change around March?
qa.a: She likely saw that it was no longer only grief for Jagdish Sir but a sadness spreading into everything, so she acted quickly.

grounding: It shows a teenager whose grief for a coach mixes anger, guilt and ashamed laughter, and whose family seeks help when the sadness spreads to everything.
